newsitem.title: UK: Metal markets rally as gloom lifts but doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: Metal markets rally as gloom lifts but doubts remain.

text.p: Prices of both industrial and precious metals moved higher on Wednesday as the mood of gloom and doom which prevailed earlier in the week lifted slightly. Explaining gold's price bounce amid a month-old downtrend, one dealer said: "It's been too bearish to be true recently and when everyone's bearish, it tends to go the other way."
Gold closed at $380.60 an ounce in London, compared to $378.65 on Tuesday.
But dealers said it was meeting selling just above the key $380 level despite a bout of short covering, which occurs when market expectations that prices will head lower reverse.
And they cautioned that gold was eventually likely to retest recent 18-month lows and then drop further.
Certainty about ever-sliding prices also waivered on the London Metal Exchange (LME), where metal values edged higher with copper leading the way and breaking back above $1,900 a tonne.
Little emerged in the way of fundamental impetus for copper but traders noted a dispute at the Tsumeb smelter in Namibia was continuing.
Aluminium rose to around $1,376, up $8.50, after it had become oversold. "Once the rally stalls, it could return to test $1,350/60," one trader said.
In contrast to the major metal markets, agricultural commodities had a mixed day.
Coffee finished at the day's highs, lifted by a fresh rally in New York. London's key November futures contract ended up $9 at $1,512.
But cocoa prices slid across the board with no news from origins or consumers to encourage fresh interest and raise modest volume. The March contract was down five stg at 993 stg.

Sugar was slightly ahead on the December contract after the New York opening but it failed to react to news of tenders results from Tunisia and Jordan. The result of Syrian and Sri Lankan tenders were not expected until Thursday.
Grains mainly took their lead from the reaction of the Chicago soybean futures to reports of possible freezing weather later in the week in the northern Midwest growing region.
Soybeans were between 3-3/4 to 6-1/2 a bushel higher at the Chicago Board of Trade midsession when December corn futures were unchanged at $2.96 a bushel.
Spring wheat was generally high on spillover in sentiment from the soybean pit.
